1.pericope_label: And it came to pass, when the king sat in his house, and the Lord had given him rest round about from all his enemies; That the king said unto Nathan the prophet, See now, I dwell in an house of cedar, but the ark of God dwelleth within curtains. And Nathan said to the king, Go, do all that is in thine heart; for the Lord is with thee.

schools.summary: Ellicott holds that the narrative stands here not because it followed chronologically but because it is closely related in subject, and dates it after the successful close of David's principal foreign wars, more likely in a time of quiet prosperity than in his latter troubles. He takes the first mention of Nathan as no sign of obscurity, since he was already a confidential counsellor and he and Gad wrote parts of the history of this reign and the next, and he notes that although the word for curtains is the one used in Exodus of the tabernacle covering, the ark was not now within that but in a similar temporary structure. Of Nathan's approval he says only that the prophet naturally thought the pious purpose must be right but spoke by his own sense of right and not by divine direction. Delitzsch lays out the shape of what follows, the desire, the refusal with its counter-promise, and the prayer of thanksgiving.

Gill observes that who Nathan was and whence he came is not known, though he was plainly a man of great piety and prudence, familiar with David and perhaps dwelling in his palace, and he reports a Jewish tradition identifying him with a nephew of David which he thinks not very likely. On the approval he is severe: since the time and the person were not pointed out in the word of God, David and Nathan should have consulted the Lord, and in this they erred and were tacitly reproved.

Clarke places the rest earlier and narrower than Ellicott does, after the Philistines were cast out of the strong places they held in Israel but before he carried his arms beyond the land against the Moabites, Syrians and Idumeans, and takes the curtains simply for the tabernacle, covered with the skins of beasts. On Nathan he is mildest of all, that he judged as a pious and prudent man and not as a prophet, the prophets not being always under a divine afflatus but only at select times. Wesley is sharpest of all: Nathan hastily approved before consulting God, as both he and David ought to have done in a matter of so great moment, and therefore meets with a rebuke and is forced to acknowledge his error and recant it.

Henry draws from the rest that though David was a man of war he was for peace and did not delight in it, that he had not been long at rest nor would be long before he was at war again, and that he was in his element meditating in the law. David's thought of a house for the ark is a grateful return, since when providence has done much for us it should set us contriving what we may do for God, and a good use of leisure; Henry sets his palace against another, how different the thoughts of David sitting in his from Nebuchadnezzar's walking in his, the one full of how to glorify God and the other of the might of his own power, and adds that gracious souls cannot enjoy their own accommodations while the church is under a cloud. On the approval he allows a mistake and has God correct it: Nathan spoke as a wise and good man, agreeably to the revealed will of God though the secret will was otherwise, and where prophets mistook, as Samuel once did and Nathan here, God soon rectified it.

debates.question: When in the reign did this happen?

positions.position: After the successful close of the principal foreign wars, the narrative being placed here for subject and not for sequence
After the Philistines were cast out of Israel but before the wars against Moab, Syria and Edom

debates.question: Did Nathan do wrong in approving the purpose?

positions.position: No fault; he judged as a pious and prudent man, the prophets not being always under a divine afflatus
A mistake, which God soon rectified, as he did with Samuel
An error in both men, who should have consulted the Lord and were tacitly reproved
A hasty approval meeting with a rebuke, so that Nathan is forced to acknowledge his error and recant it

outliers.claim: Denies that the ark was in the Mosaic tabernacle at this time, holding that although the word for curtains is the one used in Exodus of that covering, the ark was in a similar but separate temporary structure

themes: And it came to pass, when the king sat in his house, and the Lord had given him rest round about from all his enemies;
That the king said unto Nathan the prophet, See now, I dwell in an house of cedar, but the ark of God dwelleth within curtains.
And Nathan said to the king, Go, do all that is in thine heart; for the Lord is with thee.

4.pericope_label: And it came to pass that night, that the word of the Lord came unto Nathan, saying, Go and tell my servant David, Thus saith the Lord, Shalt thou build me an house for me to dwell in? Whereas I have not dwelt in any house since the time that I brought up the children of Israel out of Egypt, even to this day, but have walked in a tent and in a tabernacle. In all the places wherein I have walked with all the children of Israel spake I a word with any of the tribes of Israel, whom I commanded to feed my people Israel, saying, Why build ye not me an house of cedar? Now therefore so shalt thou say unto my servant David, Thus saith the Lord of hosts, I took thee from the sheepcote, from following the sheep, to be ruler over my people, over Israel: And I was with thee whithersoever thou wentest, and have cut off all thine enemies out of thy sight, and have made thee a great name, like unto the name of the great men that are in the earth. Moreover I will appoint a place for my people Israel, and will plant them, that they may dwell in a place of their own, and move no more; neither shall the children of wickedness afflict them any more, as beforetime, And as since the time that I commanded judges to be over my people Israel, and have caused thee to rest from all thine enemies. Also the Lord telleth thee that he will make thee an house.

schools.summary: Ellicott makes the decisive point on why David was refused: no reason is given here, calling David my servant shows the prohibition carried no divine displeasure, and the only reason assigned anywhere is the one David himself gives later, that he had shed much blood and been a man of war, wars that were necessary and never disapproved but which still unfitted him for the office. He then rejects the two reasons nearly all commentators find in the message itself, that God must first build David a house and that the kingdom was not yet settled, on the ground that neither is assigned in the divine word. He also reads the tenses of the promise to Israel as past rather than future and keeps the received tribes against the parallel's judges. Delitzsch offers precisely the two reasons Ellicott rejects, calling the first not a mere play upon words but the deep general truth that God must first build a man's house before the man can build God's, and reads the pairing of tent and dwelling as one thing, observing that since a tent is a traveller's dwelling God appeared as if himself travelling.

Gill explains the timing, that the answer came that same night so that neither man should continue long in his error, and holds with Wesley that the parenthesis about Israel should close before the clause about rest, which concerns David alone.

Clarke says the interrogative has the force of thou shalt not, prefers the parallel's judges to the received tribes since the two Hebrew words differ by a single stroke that would be mistaken if a little effaced, and agrees with Ellicott that the tenses should be past, I have appointed a place and have planted them. Wesley distinguishes tent from tabernacle where Delitzsch runs them together, the one the curtains and hangings within and the other the frame of boards and its coverings, keeps the future tense, and alone enters a condition on the promise to Israel, that it holds except they notoriously forsake God.

Henry supplies a reason for the refusal that no one else gives, a division of labour: David is a man of war who must enlarge the borders, and a sweet psalmist who must prepare psalms and settle the courses of the Levites, while his son's genius will better suit the building. He also explains why the word came by Nathan rather than directly, since one prophet countermanding another would have left Nathan despised and David perplexed, and God chose to support the honour of his prophets. On the tent he is fullest: God regards not outward pomp, and his presence was as surely with his people when the ark was in a tent; David calls the tabernacle a temple in the psalms because it answered the intention of one though made of curtains, and may have had sweeter communion in a house of curtains than any successor in the house of cedar; from God's silence to the rulers he concludes that only instituted worship is acceptable, and that a tent of God's appointing is better than a temple of one's own inventing.

debates.question: Why was David not allowed to build?

positions.position: For no reason given here; the only reason assigned anywhere is that he was a man of blood, and the reasons commentators supply should be refused
Because God must first build a man's house before the man can build God's, and because the land was still disputed
By a division of labour, David having wars to fight and psalms to prepare while his son was fitter for building

debates.question: Did God speak to the tribes or to the judges?

positions.position: Judges, as the parallel reads, the two Hebrew words differing by a single stroke
Tribes, the same usage for the judges sprung from them occurring elsewhere

debates.question: Are the verbs about a place for Israel past or future?

positions.position: Past: I have appointed a place and have planted them
Future, as the received version has it

outliers.claim: Concludes from God never having asked any ruler for a cedar house that only instituted worship is acceptable, and that a tent of God's appointing is better than a temple of one's own inventing

12.pericope_label: And when thy days be fulfilled, and thou shalt sleep with thy fathers, I will set up thy seed after thee, which shall proceed out of thy bowels, and I will establish his kingdom. He shall build an house for my name, and I will stablish the throne of his kingdom for ever. I will be his father, and he shall be my son. If he commit iniquity, I will chasten him with the rod of men, and with the stripes of the children of men: But my mercy shall not depart away from him, as I took it from Saul, whom I put away before thee. And thine house and thy kingdom shall be established for ever before thee: thy throne shall be established for ever. According to all these words, and according to all this vision, so did Nathan speak unto David.

schools.summary: Ellicott notes that many take the future tense about the seed as proof that Solomon was not yet born, which would fix the point in the reign, but that the same expression might have been used afterwards, the future being an assimilation to the futures running through the passage. His rule for the promise is succession rather than division: it plainly has a human successor in view, yet the establishment for ever, repeated three times, can only be fulfilled in the Messiah, and the case is the same as with the prophet promised through Moses, a long line of men filling the place of the true Prophet and King and all culminating in him. He observes that two different Hebrew words stand behind the one word established, the second better rendered made sure, refuses the Greek alteration of before thee into before me, and reads the verse as the last narrowing of an old promise given first to the race, then to Abraham's nation, then to Judah, and now to David's family. Delitzsch says it is very obvious from all the details that the promise related primarily to Solomon, insists that the rod of men means the punishments inflicted on all men who go astray and not the moderate correction of a parent, and holds that the vision was had waking and at night and not in a dream.

Gill keeps Solomon and the Messiah in view together, Solomon building the house and his antitype building another, and Solomon a son by adopting grace where Christ is Son by natural and eternal generation. On the mercy that shall not depart he is careful to say it is not special grace but the kind of mercy that can be taken away, as it was from Saul.

Clarke takes the throne established for ever as the government of the spiritual kingdom, and draws the contrast with Saul to its end, that Saul's family became totally extinct while David's remained until the incarnation, Joseph and Mary being both of it, so that Jesus was the only heir, who did not choose the secular throne but ascended the spiritual one. He adds a warning of another kind, that many have used these verses to support unconditional final perseverance, that the text has nothing to do with it, and that pressing it would ruin the doctrine, since there is neither proof nor evidence of Solomon's salvation. Wesley states the sharpest rule for dividing the promise: some of it belongs to David's posterity in general, some to Solomon, some to Christ only, and where Solomon was a type the sense passes through him to Christ, but the clause about committing iniquity cannot touch Christ and is therefore terminated in Solomon. On the rod of men he reads gentle and moderate correction suited to man's weakness.

Henry reads the rod of men as Wesley does and prefers the softer of two senses, either a rod such as men may wield, so that God will not plead against him with his great power, or rather one such as men may bear, God considering his frame and correcting with all tenderness, not a stroke or a wound but a gentle touch.

debates.question: How is the promise divided between Solomon and the Messiah?

positions.position: By parts, some clauses terminating in Solomon and others passing through him to Christ
By succession, a long line of human heads of the theocracy all culminating in the Messiah
Primarily to Solomon, as all the separate details make obvious
Both together throughout, Solomon and his antitype the Messiah

debates.question: What is the rod of men?

positions.position: The punishments inflicted on all men who go astray, from which the seed of David is not excepted
Gentle and moderate correction suited to man's weakness, a touch rather than a wound

debates.question: What kind of revelation was the vision?

positions.position: One had waking and at night, the term being constantly distinguished from the word for a dream
Any divine communication, not vision strictly so called

outliers.claim: Warns that these verses have often been pressed to support unconditional final perseverance, that the text has nothing to do with the doctrine, and that pressing it would ruin it, since there is neither proof nor evidence of Solomon's salvation

18.pericope_label: Then went king David in, and sat before the Lord, and he said, Who am I, O Lord God? and what is my house, that thou hast brought me hitherto? And this was yet a small thing in thy sight, O Lord God; but thou hast spoken also of thy servant’s house for a great while to come. And is this the manner of man, O Lord God? And what can David say more unto thee? for thou, Lord God, knowest thy servant. For thy word’s sake, and according to thine own heart, hast thou done all these great things, to make thy servant know them. Wherefore thou art great, O Lord God: for there is none like thee, neither is there any God beside thee, according to all that we have heard with our ears. And what one nation in the earth is like thy people, even like Israel, whom God went to redeem for a people to himself, and to make him a name, and to do for you great things and terrible, for thy land, before thy people, which thou redeemedst to thee from Egypt, from the nations and their gods? For thou hast confirmed to thyself thy people Israel to be a people unto thee for ever: and thou, Lord, art become their God.

schools.summary: Delitzsch denies that David sat at all, since the verb means remained or tarried and the custom of sitting before the Lord in prayer cannot be deduced from the one passage usually cited, where Moses is made to sit by exhaustion. Ellicott lets the sitting stand as meditation before thanksgiving, praise and prayer, and does the chapter's hardest textual work on the clause our version turns into a question about the manner of men: the Hebrew is obscure, the versions give little help, the word rendered manner never bears that sense elsewhere and means law, and no question is intended, so the line should read as an exclamation, and this is a law for man. On the plural verb in the verse about redemption he explains that the plural name always takes a singular verb when it means the true God, so the plural here means what nation is there whom its gods went to redeem; and he works two further difficulties in the same verse, the words for you, dropped by the Greek and altered by the Latin, and for thy land, where the Greek and the parallel have by driving out. He also holds it unnecessary to confine what David heard with his ears to oral tradition, since the same word is used of written records.
Gill notes only that David went into the tabernacle he had prepared for the ark.

Clarke supplies an eastern parallel for the posture, that a suppliant seeking a favour seats himself in silence before a superior, or before the idol in a waiting posture, and renders the hard clause more literally still as the law of Adam, asking whether David reaches back to the promise that the seed of the woman should bruise the serpent's head, so that from his line the Messiah should spring. Wesley takes the middle way on the posture, that David sat for a season while meditating and then altered it; he keeps the clause as a question and answers it, that men do not use their inferiors so and this is the prerogative of divine grace; and he reads the ground of the promise as faithfulness, that God might fulfil what he promised, taking according to thine own heart as mere liberality without desert and remarking how far David was from thinking his actions meritorious.

Henry reports the Jewish claim that the kings of David's house alone might sit in the temple, refuses to let it justify the gesture in ordinary prayer, and offers two escapes, that David took his place before the Lord or continued there meditating and stood up to pray. He keeps the hard clause as a question and doubles it, asking whether man can expect such dealing from his Maker and whether men deal thus with one another, but also passes on the other reading and draws a doctrine from it, that one whose kingdom is established for ever must be a man and yet the Lord Jehovah, so a Messiah from David's loins must be man but reigning for ever must be God. On the plural verb in the verse about redemption he hears the Trinity, the same consultation of all the persons about redemption as about creation; and he reads for thy word's sake either of Christ the eternal Word or of God magnifying his word of promise above all his name.

debates.question: Did David sit before the Lord?

positions.position: No; the verb means remained or tarried, and sitting as a posture of prayer cannot be deduced from the passage usually cited
Yes, sitting to meditate in God's presence
He sat while meditating and changed posture to pray

debates.question: What does the clause rendered Is this the manner of man mean?

positions.position: Not a question at all, but an exclamation, and this is a law for man
Literally the law of Adam, perhaps pointing back to the promise about the seed of the woman
A question, and also a statement that the promised king must be man and yet the Lord Jehovah
A question about how men treat their inferiors, answered by the prerogative of divine grace

debates.question: Why is the verb plural where God goes to redeem Israel?

positions.position: Because the thought is what nation is there whom its gods went to redeem, the true God always taking a singular verb
Because the persons of the Trinity consulted together about redemption as about creation

outliers.claim: Holds it unnecessary to confine what David had heard with his ears to oral tradition, since the same word is used elsewhere of written records, so that David means the history of God's dealings as recorded in their sacred books

25.pericope_label: And now, O Lord God, the word that thou hast spoken concerning thy servant, and concerning his house, establish it for ever, and do as thou hast said. And let thy name be magnified for ever, saying, The Lord of hosts is the God over Israel: and let the house of thy servant David be established before thee. For thou, O Lord of hosts, God of Israel, hast revealed to thy servant, saying, I will build thee an house: therefore hath thy servant found in his heart to pray this prayer unto thee. And now, O Lord God, thou art that God, and thy words be true, and thou hast promised this goodness unto thy servant: Therefore now let it please thee to bless the house of thy servant, that it may continue for ever before thee: for thou, O Lord God, hast spoken it: and with thy blessing let the house of thy servant be blessed for ever.

schools.summary: Ellicott suggests the closing words may be a future rather than a wish, a prophecy built on the promise rather than a petition, and notes that although several psalms have been referred to this point in David's life, none carries a note of time fixing it here, unless the one that reads like an inspired interpretation of the promise of perpetuity. On the petition that God's name be magnified he observes that David puts the hallowing of the name first, in the true spirit of the Lord's Prayer, and that this was the striking feature of his whole life whatever sins he was betrayed into. Delitzsch divides the prayer into thanksgiving for the promise and supplication for its fulfilment, and finds the two summed up again in the clauses beginning with and now.

Gill passes on the Targum's rendering of the last request as begin and bless, so that the promised blessings might begin to descend and give some encouragement that the whole would be fulfilled, and makes the petition for the magnifying of the name turn on the Messiah.

Clarke turns this section into the longest argument in the chapter. He insists the promises were conditional, so that they have failed to David's natural posterity and are fulfilled to Christ and his spiritual seed alone; he answers a deistical writer's three objections to finding a Messianic promise here, by reading the verbs of the promise to Israel as past, by making the house a spiritual family raised up after David slept with his fathers, which excludes Solomon, and by rendering the clause about iniquity passively, as suffering for iniquity with the rod due to men. From this he concludes that the prophecy cannot admit a double sense or be applied to two such opposite characters. He also draws a general rule from David's exclusion, that God seldom employs a soldier in spiritual work for the same reason, illustrating it from a dragoon turned preacher who reformed many hundreds in the army and was persuaded he had never killed a man. Wesley reduces the petition for the name to its plainest sense, that God should never cease to manifest himself as the God and governor of Israel.

Henry notices that David returned his answer to God himself rather than sending it by Nathan, since when ministers deliver God's message it is not to them but to God that our hearts must reply, and grounds the petitions on the message, David asking only what God has already revealed.

debates.question: Can the promise be read of both Solomon and the Messiah?

positions.position: No; if the Messiah is meant, suffering innocently for others, Solomon cannot be, and no double sense is admissible
Yes, by succession, division or type, as the rest of the chapter reads it

debates.question: Are the closing words a petition or a prophecy?

positions.position: Possibly a future, a prophecy built on the promise
A petition, and on the Targum a request that the blessing begin now

outliers.claim: Generalises David's exclusion into a rule that God seldom employs a soldier in spiritual work for the same reason, illustrating it from a dragoon turned preacher who reformed many hundreds in the army and was persuaded that in all his battles he had never killed a man
